title: Is Winter Disappearing Faster Than Summer Is Warming?
research_question: How do the rates of winter and summer warming differ across geographic regions, and how might these seasonal differences change under future emissions scenarios?

method: Meteorological Northern Hemisphere seasons: DJF assigned to January/February year, JJA to calendar year. All three months required, weighted by calendar days. Winter 1995 uses December 1994. Winter 2015 joins historical December 2014 to scenario January–February 2015. Winter 2100 uses December 2099, not December 2100. Each cell’s season-specific mean of 20 seasons in 1995–2014 is subtracted. Regions use spherical area of published cell bounds, with fractional latitude and longitude overlap. Period means weight complete season-years equally. Warming rate is ordinary least-squares slope × 10, in °C/decade, with the same years for winter and summer. Trend displays require at least 20 consecutive future season-years.
limitations: One model and member, no ensemble uncertainty or significance test. North America and Europe are rectangular sectors, not continent masks, and include ocean. Arctic overlaps the northern parts of the other sectors. No snow, frost-day or winter-length data are used. Disappearing is a narrative hook: this does not measure literal disappearance of winter. Spatially varying baseline is recent, not preindustrial. Seasonal anomaly difference is not the same measure as a warming-rate difference.
